title: Atlassian puts its engineers on an AI budget as the cost of ‘tokenmaxxing’ bites
excerpt: The software maker cut thousands of jobs in the name of AI. Now it is handing the engineers who remain capped ‘AI wallets,’ a sign the industry’s token spending has become a line item to manage. Atlassian has started giving its engineers a fixed monthly allowance for artificial intelligence, a capped “AI wallet” that warns […]
content_html:
The software maker cut thousands of jobs in the name of AI. Now it is handing the engineers who remain capped ‘AI wallets,’ a sign the industry’s token spending has become a line item to manage.

Atlassian has started giving its engineers a fixed monthly allowance for artificial intelligence, a capped “AI wallet” that warns them as they near the limit and stops when the budget runs out.

The move places the software company on the cost-conscious side of a growing divide over how much AI staff should be allowed to burn through.

The caps are not trivial, but they are caps. Atlassian’s wallets run from $500 to $2,000 a month for research-and-development staff, with the size set by role and the option to ask for more, a structure meant to keep spending visible rather than to starve it.

The company frames it as generosity with guardrails. “Atlassian provides a significant budget for our builders to leverage multiple AI tools,” a spokesperson said, casting the wallet as a way to fund experimentation without letting the bills run wild.

There is an irony in the metering, and it is not a small one. Atlassian has recast itself as an “AI-first” company, cutting 1,600 jobs to fund the pivot, and earlier in the year it told a group of support staff, over video, that they would be largely replaced by AI.

Now it is rationing that same AI for the people who kept their jobs. Having sold the technology as efficient enough to replace workers, the company is finding it is also expensive enough to need a budget, which is a harder line to put on a motivational slide.

Coding agents that once cost pennies now run tasks that consume tokens by the million, and the practice of maximising that usage, nicknamed “tokenmaxxing,” has turned individual engineers into meaningful cost centres.

The arithmetic explains the anxiety. A token is roughly four characters of text, and at prevailing prices of several dollars per million tokens for the leading models, an agent left to iterate on its own can run up a large bill, the kind of dynamic that has already broken the economics of tools like GitHub Copilot.

Atlassian is not the first to react. Amazon quietly shut down an internal leaderboard that had turned heavy AI use into a competition, after employees gamed it by consuming tokens for their own sake.

Meta went further still; the company warned some 6,000 staff that its internal AI spending in 2026 could reach into the billions, and began rolling out token budgets and controls of the kind Atlassian has now adopted.

If last year’s fashion was tokenmaxxing, this year’s is its opposite, a turn toward treating AI spend as something to manage rather than a badge of how forward-leaning a team is.

The reversal is awkward for an industry that spent two years urging staff to use more AI. Executives who once measured adoption by token volume are now measuring it by cost per outcome, a soberer metric that fits a moment of tighter budgets.

Not everyone is pulling back. Some firms still offer unlimited AI budgets as a recruiting perk and a bet on productivity, wagering that the output justifies the spend and that capping it would only slow their best engineers.

That is the real disagreement beneath the wallets. No one doubts the tools are useful; the fight is over whether unlimited access produces enough extra value to be worth an unpredictable, fast-rising bill.

Atlassian’s answer is a middle path. By funding multiple tools but metering their use, it is trying to keep the productivity of agentic AI while stripping out the waste, a balance the whole sector is now hunting for.

Whether that produces better engineering or merely cheaper engineering is the open question.

For now, a company that thinned its workforce in the name of AI is asking the survivors to watch every token, having learned that the technology it sold as a way to do more with fewer people is not, as it turns out, free.

这家软件制造商以人工智能的名义裁员数千人。 现在，它正在向仍受限制的工程师提供“人工智能钱包”，这表明该行业的代币支出已成为需要管理的项目。

Atlassian 已开始为其工程师提供每月固定的人工智能津贴，这是一个有上限的“人工智能钱包”，当他们接近限额时会发出警告，并在预算用完时停止。

此举使这家软件公司处于成本意识的一方，因为对于应允许多少人工智能员工被解雇的分歧日益扩大。

这些上限并不是微不足道的，但它们就是上限。 Atlassian 为研发人员提供的薪酬从每月 500 美元到 2,000 美元不等，其规模根据角色设定，并可以选择要求更多，这种结构旨在保持支出可见，而不是让支出挨饿。

该公司将其描述为带有护栏的慷慨。 一位发言人表示：“Atlassian 为我们的开发者提供了大量预算来利用多种人工智能工具。”他将钱包视为一种资助实验的方式，同时又不会让账单疯狂。

欧盟科技的💜

测光中有讽刺，而且还不是小事。 Atlassian 将自己重塑为一家“人工智能优先”的公司，裁员 1,600 人，为转型提供资金，并在今年早些时候通过视频告诉一群支持人员，他们将在很大程度上被人工智能取代。

现在，它正在为保住工作的人配给同样的人工智能。 该公司出售的技术效率足以取代工人，但它也发现它的成本也足够昂贵，需要预算，而这对于激励幻灯片来说是一个更难的路线。

曾经花费几分钱的编码代理现在运行消耗数百万代币的任务，而最大化使用的实践（绰号为“tokenmaxxing”）已将单个工程师变成了有意义的成本中心。

算术解释了焦虑。 一个代币大约是四个字符的文本，对于领先模型来说，按照每百万代币几美元的普遍价格，一个自行迭代的代理可能会产生巨额费用，这种动态已经打破了 GitHub Copilot 等工具的经济性。

Atlassian 并不是第一个做出反应的。 亚马逊悄悄关闭了一个内部排行榜，该排行榜将人工智能的大量使用变成了一场竞争，此前员工为了自己的利益而消费代币来玩游戏。

梅塔走得更远；该公司警告约 6,000 名员工，2026 年其内部人工智能支出可能达到数十亿美元，并开始推出 Atlassian 目前采用的那种代币预算和控制措施。

如果说去年的时尚是代币最大化，那么今年的时尚则恰恰相反，将人工智能支出视为需要管理的东西，而不是团队是否具有前瞻性的标志。

对于一个花了两年时间敦促员工更多使用人工智能的行业来说，这种逆转是尴尬的。 曾经通过代币数量来衡量采用率的高管现在通过每个结果的成本来衡量，这是一个适合预算紧张时期的冷静指标。

并非所有人都在撤退。 一些公司仍然提供无限的人工智能预算，作为招聘福利和对生产力的赌注，押注产出证明支出是合理的，而限制预算只会减慢他们最好的工程师的速度。

这才是钱包下面真正的分歧。 没有人怀疑这些工具的有用性；争论的焦点是无限制的访问是否能产生足够的额外价值，足以抵得上不可预测、快速上涨的账单。

Atlassian 的答案是一条中间道路。 通过资助多种工具并计量其使用，它试图保持代理人工智能的生产力，同时消除浪费，这是整个行业现在正在寻求的平衡。

这是否会产生更好的工程或仅仅是更便宜的工程，这是一个悬而未决的问题。

目前，一家以人工智能名义精简员工的公司正在要求幸存者关注每一个代币，因为它了解到，它出售的技术是为了用更少的人做更多的事情，但事实证明，它并不是免费的。
